The publisher shares the broker's connection, from startup to shutdown. fn service(broker: SqsBroker, queue: String) -> (impl App<State = ()>, SqsPublisher) { let intake = broker.publisher(); let app = RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber(Unnamed::<SqsQueue>::new(), Receive) .build() .name(queue) .create_if_missing(), ); }); (app, intake) }

Startup opens every subscription: it resolves the queue URL, reads the queue's visibility timeout and writes a declared redrive policy. Each subscription first checks its descriptor, before any call to AWS. An empty queue name, a wait above 20 seconds or a visibility outside one second to twelve hours fails startup with SqsError::InvalidQueue. The subscription then resolves the queue name to its URL with GetQueueUrl, once, and the broker caches the answer. A queue URL in the descriptor is used as it is. A queue that does not exist fails startup with SqsError::Queue, naming the queue, unless the subscription creates it. A registration with a redrive policy writes the policy onto the queue next. A subscription that names no visibility reads the queue's own timeout with GetQueueAttributes, and holds every delivery under it. Every request runs under the per-attempt timeout of 25 seconds that new sets on connect. A broker built from a config runs under the timeouts that config carries. The first request also fetches the credentials, so a missing credential or an unreachable endpoint fails startup too. The in-process account a TestApp test runs on has every queue the service names, so a missing queue shows only against a running stack. A descriptor out of range fails TestApp::start as it fails a real startup.

The subscription reads a queue the infrastructure created, and takes its visibility timeout from the queue. Macros Manual examples/sqs_broker_startup.rs #[subscriber(SqsQueue)] async fn handle(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order received"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Reads `queue`, which the infrastructure creates. The subscription names no visibility /// timeout, so startup reads the queue's own. fn service(broker: SqsBroker, queue: String) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(handle.name(queue).wait(Duration::from_secs(20))); }) } examples/manual/sqs_broker_startup.rs struct Receive; impl Handle<Order> for Receive { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order received"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// Reads `queue`, which the infrastructure creates. The subscription names no visibility /// timeout, so startup reads the queue's own. fn service(broker: SqsBroker, queue: String) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber(Unnamed::<SqsQueue>::new(), Receive) .build() .name(queue) .wait(Duration::from_secs(20)), ); }) }

A delivery carries its payload and its headers; each header is one SQS message attribute, String or Binary, at most ten. A header the service takes as text travels as a String attribute, and any other value as a Binary one. A handler reads the same bytes either way, and never sees which type carried them. No envelope wraps the message, so any other SQS producer or consumer reads it as it is. SQS and SNS take at most ten attributes on one message. A publish that needs more fails before it is sent, with SqsError::TooManyAttributes: it names the destination, the count, the limit, the attributes, and the one the crate added, if it added one. An attribute name is 1 to 256 letters, digits, _, - and ., and a value is never empty. A message SQS refuses fails the publish with SqsError::Publish, and the in-process account refuses it the same way. A message is at most 1 MiB, body and attributes together. A handler reads the headers as a typed contract with Headers<T>, or one by one through cx.headers(). Two headers have meanings of their own: RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER carries the queue's receive count, and PARTITION_KEY_HEADER the FIFO message group. A payload SQS would not take as text travels base64-encoded with one more attribute, as the body page describes. The crate adds no per-delivery context field, so a handler takes no Ctx<K> parameter here; what a delivery carries beyond its payload is in its headers.

An order carries its tenant and a trace id as two message attributes, and the handler reads them as one contract. Macros Manual examples/sqs_delivery_headers.rs /// The headers an order carries: two message attributes on the queue. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize)] struct OrderMeta { tenant: String, trace: Option<String>, } #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("orders"))] async fn bill(order: &Order, Headers(meta): Headers<OrderMeta>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, meta.tenant, trace = ?meta.trace, "order billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_delivery_headers.rs /// The headers an order carries: two message attributes on the queue. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct OrderMeta { tenant: String, trace: Option<String>, } struct Bill; impl Handle<Message<OrderMeta, Order>> for Bill { fn handle( &self, msg: &Message<OrderMeta, Order>, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let (order, meta) = (&msg.body, &msg.headers); tracing::info!(order.id, meta.tenant, trace = ?meta.trace, "order billed"); ready(Ok(())) } }

SQS bodies are text, so a payload SQS would refuse travels base64 with a marker attribute and is decoded again on receive. SQS takes a narrower set of characters than UTF-8 in a body. It refuses the control characters other than tab, line feed and carriage return, and the two non-characters at the end of the basic plane. A payload that is such text, a JSON document for one, travels as it is. Any other payload travels base64-encoded, with the attribute ruststream-payload-encoding set to base64: bytes that are not UTF-8, and equally valid UTF-8 with control characters, which a binary codec often emits. The receiving side decodes the body again before the handler sees it. A handler receives the bytes the producer published, and the marker attribute never reaches its headers. An attribute of that name with any other value is not the marker, and it arrives as a header. The marker counts towards the ten attributes of a message, so a binary payload leaves nine for the service's own headers. A publish with a header named ruststream-payload-encoding fails with SqsError::InvalidHeader, because the receiving side would take it for the marker. SQS refuses an empty body, and so does the in-process account. A handler that reads the bytes itself takes a #[derive(Deserialized)] newtype over &[u8], and no codec runs. The type borrows the delivery's buffer, so nothing is copied.

The handler stores thumbnails, raw image bytes that SQS would not take as text. Macros Manual examples/sqs_delivery_body.rs /// A thumbnail as the producer sent it: raw image bytes, read without a codec. #[derive(Deserialized)] struct Thumbnail<'a>(&'a [u8]); #[subscriber(SqsQueue)] async fn store(thumbnail: &Thumbnail<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(bytes = thumbnail.0.len(), "thumbnail stored"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_delivery_body.rs /// A thumbnail as the producer sent it: raw image bytes, read without a codec. struct Thumbnail<'a>(&'a [u8]); impl Deserialized for Thumbnail<'_> { type Output<'a> = Thumbnail<'a>; type Error = Infallible; fn from_payload(payload: &[u8]) -> Result<Thumbnail<'_>, Self::Error> { Ok(Thumbnail(payload)) } } // Routes the type onto the lane of payloads that read themselves. impl Input for Thumbnail<'_> { type Axis = SoloDeserialized<Thumbnail<'static>>; } struct Store; // For every lifetime of the payload it borrows. impl<'p> Handle<Thumbnail<'p>> for Store { fn handle( &self, thumbnail: &Thumbnail<'p>, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(bytes = thumbnail.0.len(), "thumbnail stored"); ready(Ok(())) } }

PARTITION_KEY_HEADER is the portable spelling of the FIFO message group: sent as MessageGroupId on a FIFO queue, as an ordinary attribute on a standard one, and read back on delivery either way. The header's name is partition-key, the one the core's in-memory broker uses, so a service that sets it runs unchanged on another broker. A publish to a .fifo queue or topic sends it as the message group, not as an attribute, and a delivery from a FIFO queue carries the group back in it. A standard queue or topic has no message groups, so there the header travels as an ordinary String attribute and counts toward the ten a message carries; a delivery carries it back as the same header. The group of a FIFO publish resolves from the most specific setting: the call's own group_id step, then this header, then the group the publish policy fixed. A FIFO publish that names none goes under the group default. SQS hands out one group's messages in order, and holds the group back while one of its messages is in flight, as the FIFO page describes.

The router forwards each order to the packing line in the customer's group, and the packer reads the group back. Macros Manual examples/sqs_delivery_partition_key.rs /// Forwards each order to the packing line in the customer's message group, so one customer's /// orders are packed in the order they were placed. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("orders"))] async fn route(order: &Order, Out(packing): Out<impl Publisher, Packing>) -> HandlerOutcome { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, order.customer.clone()); match packing .message(order) .to("packing.fifo") .with_headers(headers) .publish() .await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } /// Reads the group back from the delivery. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("packing.fifo"))] async fn pack(order: &Order, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let group = cx .headers() .get(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER) .map(String::from_utf8_lossy); tracing::info!(order.id, ?group, "order packed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_delivery_partition_key.rs /// Forwards each order to the packing line in the customer's message group, so one customer's /// orders are packed in the order they were placed. struct Route; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Route where Entry: OutEntry<Packing, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, order.customer.clone()); let sent = outs .get(Packing) .message(order) .to("packing.fifo") .with_headers(headers) .publish() .await; sent.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } /// Reads the group back from the delivery. struct Pack; impl Handle<Order> for Pack { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let group = ctx .headers() .get(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER) .map(String::from_utf8_lossy); tracing::info!(order.id, ?group, "order packed"); ready(Ok(())) } }

RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER carries the queue's ApproximateReceiveCount, one on the first delivery, so a handler can tell the last attempt. The header's name is sqs-receive-count, and its value is the count as decimal text. SQS counts every receive of a message, the one in hand included. A retry or a deferred retry returns the message to the same queue, so the count goes on rising. A redrive policy caps the same count. After max_attempts receives, SQS moves the message to the dead-letter queue on the receive that follows. A handler that compares the header with the cap knows when it holds the last attempt. SQS calls the count approximate: on a standard queue a message is delivered at least once, and a duplicate receive counts too.

A declined payment is tried three times. On the third receive the handler sends it to review and acknowledges it, so it never reaches the dead-letter queue. Macros Manual examples/sqs_delivery_receive_count.rs /// How many times the queue hands a payment over before it moves it to the dead-letter queue. const ATTEMPTS: u32 = 3; #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("payments"))] async fn charge( payment: &Payment, cx: &mut Context<'_>, Out(review): Out<impl Publisher, Review>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { if payment.card_accepted { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } let receives: u32 = cx .headers() .get(RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER) .and_then(|count| str::from_utf8(count).ok()?.parse().ok()) .unwrap_or(1); if receives < ATTEMPTS { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } // The last attempt: a person looks at the payment before the queue gives up on it. tracing::warn!(payment.id, receives, "payment declined, sent to review"); match review .message(payment) .to("payments-review") .publish() .await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } #[app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(SqsBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(charge) .max_attempts(nonzero!(ATTEMPTS)) .dead_letter("payments-dead") .out(Review, Publish::default()) .build(); }) } examples/manual/sqs_delivery_receive_count.rs /// How many times the queue hands a payment over before it moves it to the dead-letter queue. const ATTEMPTS: u32 = 3; struct Charge; impl<Entry> Handle<Payment, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Charge where Entry: OutEntry<Review, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if payment.card_accepted { return Ok(()); } let receives: u32 = ctx .headers() .get(RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER) .and_then(|count| str::from_utf8(count).ok()?.parse().ok()) .unwrap_or(1); if receives < ATTEMPTS { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } // The last attempt: a person looks at the payment before the queue gives up on it. tracing::warn!(payment.id, receives, "payment declined, sent to review"); let sent = outs .get(Review) .message(payment) .to("payments-review") .publish() .await; sent.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(SqsBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber(Unnamed::<SqsQueue>::new(), Charge) .build() .name("payments"), ) .max_attempts(nonzero!(ATTEMPTS)) .dead_letter("payments-dead") .out(Review, Publish::default()) .build(); }) }

SqsPublish, Publish in the prelude, sends each message to the queue it names; it is the broker's default, so a reply needs no policy. A mount site names it wherever a registration publishes: .out(Slot, Publish::default()) for a slot, .out_reply(Publish::default()) for a reply. A lifecycle hook takes it too, b.after_startup(Publish::default(), ..), and is handed the live publisher. The policy holds no connection; the runtime pairs it with the connected broker at startup into an SqsPublisher. A registration that names no policy for its reply publishes through this one, so .out_reply(Publish::default()) only restates the default. The destination is a queue name or a queue URL. A name resolves to its URL through GetQueueUrl, and the broker caches the answer. A publish never creates a queue: a name the account lacks fails the publish with an error. A publish returns once SQS has accepted the message, or with the error SQS reported. The payload is the message body, and the headers travel as message attributes. SQS takes a message of up to 1 MiB, body and attributes together. On a .fifo queue every send carries a message group and a deduplication id. A handler sets either for one message through SqsPublishOptions. SnsPublish sends the same messages to an SNS topic instead.

The confirmation names its queue, and the mount site binds no policy for the reply. Macros Manual examples/sqs_publishing_publish.rs /// The confirmation names its queue, so every reply of this type lands there. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "confirmations")] struct Confirmation { order_id: u64, } #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("orders"), reply)] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); Confirmation { order_id: order.id } } fn service(broker: SqsBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // No `.out_reply(..)`: the reply rides the broker's default policy, `Publish`. b.include(confirm); }) } examples/manual/sqs_publishing_publish.rs /// The confirmation names its queue, so every reply of this type lands there. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[outgoing(name = "confirmations")] struct Confirmation { order_id: u64, } struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); ready(Ok(Confirmation { order_id: order.id })) } } fn service(broker: SqsBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // No `.out_reply(..)`: the reply rides the broker's default policy, `Publish`. b.include(subscriber("orders", Confirm).reply().build()); }) }

deduplication_id names one message's idempotency key on a FIFO destination; left unnamed, every send gets a process-unique id. A FIFO queue accepts a message whose deduplication id it has seen in the last five minutes and does not deliver it again. The repeated publish succeeds, so the sender cannot tell the two apart and does not need to. An id derived from the input makes a handler's publish idempotent: SQS delivers a message at least once, and a second run of the handler sends the same id. The id is a step of one publish, never a setting of the policy. A constant id would collapse everything a position sends into one message. A send that names none carries an id this crate makes unique within the process, rs-<pid>-<sequence>. Two identical payloads sent on purpose therefore stay two messages, even on a queue with content-based deduplication. The step on a standard queue fails the publish with SqsError::NotFifo. A FIFO topic takes the same step through SnsPublish.

A payment SQS delivers twice leads to one charge: both runs send the charge under the payment's id. Macros Manual examples/sqs_publishing_deduplication.rs /// SQS delivers a message at least once, so this handler may run twice for one payment. Both /// runs send the charge under the payment's id, and the FIFO queue keeps the first. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("payments"))] async fn bill( payment: &Payment, Out(charges): Out<impl Publisher<Options = SqsPublishOptions>, Charges>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let charge = Charge { payment_id: payment.id, amount: payment.amount, }; let sent = charges .message(&charge) .group_id(&payment.account) .deduplication_id(format!("payment-{}", payment.id)) .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = sent { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "charge not sent"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_publishing_deduplication.rs /// SQS delivers a message at least once, so this handler may run twice for one payment. Both /// runs send the charge under the payment's id, and the FIFO queue keeps the first. struct Bill; impl<Entry> Handle<Payment, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Bill where Entry: OutEntry<Charges, Wire: Publisher<Options = SqsPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let charge = Charge { payment_id: payment.id, amount: payment.amount, }; let sent = outs .get(Charges) .message(&charge) .group_id(&payment.account) .deduplication_id(format!("payment-{}", payment.id)) .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = sent { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "charge not sent"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } }

group_id on the policy orders everything a position publishes within one group; a call's own step and the partition key win over it. A FIFO queue delivers the messages of one group in the order they were sent, one group member at a time. Messages of different groups do not wait for each other. A group belongs to a position: a slot, a reply or a lifecycle hook. Every send from that position to a .fifo destination falls back to the group its policy fixed. Three answers can be in play at once, and the most specific wins. The call's own group_id step comes first. The message's PARTITION_KEY_HEADER comes next, the spelling that travels unchanged to every other broker. The policy's group comes last, and a send that names none at all goes under "default". A FIFO delivery carries its group in the partition-key header, which is where a handler and a test read it. A group on a position that publishes to a standard queue fails the publish with SqsError::NotFifo. A partition key alone is a portable hint: it names no group on a standard queue and travels there as an ordinary attribute. SnsPublish::group_id does the same for a FIFO topic.

At startup the service replays the orders a previous run did not hand on, all in the group replay, so fulfillment receives them in the order they were taken. The place handler names each customer's group for its own messages, which wins over its slot's policy. Macros Manual examples/sqs_fifo_group.rs fn service(broker: SqsBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(place).out(Placements, Publish::default()).build(); b.include(fulfil); // The replay keeps its own order: every message the hook sends is in the group `replay`. b.after_startup( Publish::default().group_id("replay"), async move |sqs| -> io::Result<()> { for order in pending() { sqs.message(&order) .publish() .await .map_err(io::Error::other)?; } Ok(()) }, ); }) } examples/manual/sqs_fifo_group.rs fn service(broker: SqsBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build()) .out(Placements, Publish::default()) .build(); b.include(subscriber("fulfillment.fifo", Fulfil).build()); // The replay keeps its own order: every message the hook sends is in the group `replay`. b.after_startup( Publish::default().group_id("replay"), async move |sqs| -> io::Result<()> { for order in pending() { sqs.message(&order) .publish() .await .map_err(io::Error::other)?; } Ok(()) }, ); }) }

A handler sets one message's group or deduplication id through the publish steps, bounding its slot on SqsPublishOptions. SqsPublishOptions holds the two settings one publish may differ from the next in: a message group and a deduplication id. A call site writes them through the steps of SqsPublishSteps, .group_id(..) and .deduplication_id(..) on the publish builder. A step wins over the group the policy fixed, for that one message. Both are FIFO settings: a .fifo destination takes them, and a standard one fails the publish. A handler bounds its slot as Out<impl Publisher<Options = SqsPublishOptions>, Marker>, which puts the steps in reach. The body imports ruststream_sqs_sns::prelude::*, the one handler file that globs this crate's prelude instead of the framework's. The same steps are on every publish surface of this crate: an injected slot, the publisher a lifecycle hook is handed, a fan-out publisher. A slot moved from SqsPublish to SnsPublish keeps the body that names them. A reply has no call site, so its policy is its whole answer. A test reads back what a publish asked for: tb.out::<Marker>().with_options(&SqsPublishOptions::default().group_id(..)).

Each customer's orders reach fulfillment in the order they were placed: the group of each message is the customer. Macros Manual examples/sqs_fifo_group.rs /// One customer's orders reach fulfillment in the order they were placed; different customers' /// orders do not wait for each other. The group is the customer. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("orders"))] async fn place( order: &Order, Out(placements): Out<impl Publisher<Options = SqsPublishOptions>, Placements>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let placed = OrderPlaced { id: order.id, customer: order.customer.clone(), }; let sent = placements .message(&placed) .group_id(&order.customer) .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = sent { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "order not placed"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_fifo_group.rs /// One customer's orders reach fulfillment in the order they were placed; different customers' /// orders do not wait for each other. The group is the customer. struct Place; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Place where Entry: OutEntry<Placements, Wire: Publisher<Options = SqsPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let placed = OrderPlaced { id: order.id, customer: order.customer.clone(), }; let sent = outs .get(Placements) .message(&placed) .group_id(&order.customer) .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = sent { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "order not placed"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } }

Each outcome is one SQS call: ack and drop delete the message, retry makes it visible again at once. ack deletes the message with DeleteMessage. drop deletes it too, because SQS has no call that rejects a message without deleting it. retry sets the message's visibility timeout to zero, so the next receive hands it out again. retry_after sets the timeout to a delay instead. A redelivered message is the same message: the queue counts its receives, and the handler reads the count in RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER. A delivery the service never settles, as when its process stops, makes no call, and the message comes back once its visibility timeout lapses. A redrive policy caps the receives, and the queue moves a spent message to a dead-letter queue itself. In the manual form Ok(()) acknowledges the delivery and Err(outcome) settles it with that outcome.

A malformed payment is dropped, a payment the gateway was too busy for comes back at once, and a charged one is deleted. Macros Manual examples/sqs_settlement_outcomes.rs /// One payment per delivery. A malformed payment is dropped, a busy gateway gets the payment /// again at once, and a charged payment is acknowledged. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("payments"))] async fn charge(payment: &Payment, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { if payment.amount_cents <= 0 { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "malformed payment dropped"); // DeleteMessage: the payment never comes back. return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } let attempt = cx.headers().get_str(RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); if charge_card(payment, attempt).await.is_err() { tracing::warn!(payment.id, attempt, "gateway busy"); // ChangeMessageVisibility to zero: the next receive hands it out again. return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } // DeleteMessage. HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_settlement_outcomes.rs /// One payment per delivery. A malformed payment is dropped, a busy gateway gets the payment /// again at once, and a charged payment is acknowledged. struct Charge; impl Handle<Payment> for Charge { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if payment.amount_cents <= 0 { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "malformed payment dropped"); // DeleteMessage: the payment never comes back. return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } let attempt = ctx.headers().get_str(RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); if charge_card(payment, attempt).await.is_err() { tracing::warn!(payment.id, attempt, "gateway busy"); // ChangeMessageVisibility to zero: the next receive hands it out again. return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } // DeleteMessage. Ok(()) } }

max_attempts and dead_letter together become the queue's redrive policy, and SQS moves a spent message to the dead-letter queue itself. The cap is the policy's maxReceiveCount, at most 1000, and the destination is the queue it points at. The subscription writes the policy onto its queue with SetQueueAttributes when it opens. SQS then counts the receives and carries the message away on the receive past the cap, so nothing leaves the service. A bare queue name takes the declaration the same way as an SqsQueue. Both halves are needed: a cap without a destination, or a destination without a cap, stops the service at startup with SqsError::IncompleteRedrive, which names the missing half. The dead-letter queue has to exist at startup, unless the subscription creates its queues. A FIFO queue takes a FIFO dead-letter queue, and a standard queue a standard one. A drop normally deletes the message, but on the delivery that has spent the policy it returns the message instead, because the next receive is what moves it to the dead-letter queue. The dead-letter queue is an ordinary queue, read by an ordinary subscription. The policy needs the permissions sqs:SetQueueAttributes on the queue and sqs:GetQueueAttributes on the dead-letter queue.

An invoice that is never ready is received three times and then moves to invoices-dead, where a person takes it over. Macros Manual examples/sqs_dead_letter.rs /// A handler that is never ready. Every delivery asks to come back later, so what ends the /// message is the cap: the queue hands it over three times and then moves it. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("invoices").create_if_missing())] async fn settle(invoice: &Invoice) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice is not ready yet"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK) } /// The dead-letter queue is an ordinary queue, read by an ordinary subscription. #[subscriber("invoices-dead")] async fn escalate(invoice: &Invoice) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::error!(invoice.id, "invoice escalated to a person"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_dead_letter.rs /// A handler that is never ready. retry_after(delay) sets the message's visibility to the delay, so it returns on the same queue with its receive count, within 12 hours of its receive. SQS holds a message back natively: ChangeMessageVisibility hides it for the delay, and the next receive after that hands it out again. Nothing is republished and no copy is made, so the message keeps its id, its attributes and its receive count. SQS counts whole seconds, so a fraction of a second rounds up. SQS keeps a message hidden for at most twelve hours from its receive, so the longest delay is what remains of those twelve hours. A longer delay is shortened to end with them, and the crate logs a warning that names the queue. The delay waits on the queue, not in the service, so a service that stops in the meantime loses nothing. SQS moves the message itself, so the registration names no retry publisher, and .out_retry(..) does not compile on an SqsQueue. A redrive policy counts a deferred receive like any other. In a test, tb.advance(delay) lets the delay pass on a paused clock.

An invoice whose payment has not cleared comes back five seconds later and is settled then. Macros Manual examples/sqs_settlement_retry_after.rs /// How long an invoice whose payment has not cleared waits before it is checked again. const RECHECK: Duration = Duration::from_secs(5); /// The payment of an invoice clears within seconds, so the first receive asks for the invoice /// again later and the second one settles it. #[subscriber(SqsQueue)] async fn settle(invoice: &Invoice, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { if cx.headers().get_str(RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER) == Some("1") { tracing::info!(invoice.id, "payment not cleared yet"); // ChangeMessageVisibility to five seconds: nothing is republished. return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK); } tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice settled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_settlement_retry_after.rs /// How long an invoice whose payment has not cleared waits before it is checked again. const RECHECK: Duration = Duration::from_secs(5); /// The payment of an invoice clears within seconds, so the first receive asks for the invoice /// again later and the second one settles it. struct Settle; impl Handle<Invoice> for Settle { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if ctx.headers().get_str(RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER) == Some("1") { tracing::info!(invoice.id, "payment not cleared yet"); // ChangeMessageVisibility to five seconds: nothing is republished. return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK))); } tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice settled"); ready(Ok(())) } }

SnsPublish fans a reply out from an SNS topic to every queue subscribed to it; one out_reply step switches a position to it. The policy needs the crate's sns feature. A mount site names it where a registration publishes: .out_reply(SnsPublish::default()) for a reply, .out(Slot, SnsPublish::default()) for a slot. The destination reads the same as on SqsPublish: the reply type or the mount site names it, and the policy decides whether the name is a queue or a topic. Without the step the same reply lands on a queue of that name. The runtime pairs the policy with the connected broker into an SnsPublisher. The destination is a topic name or a topic ARN. A name resolves to its ARN through CreateTopic, which returns an existing topic as it is and creates a missing one. A name ending in .fifo is a FIFO topic, and it takes the same group and deduplication steps as a FIFO queue. A topic and a queue may share a name: each publish goes where its policy sends it. The payload is the notification's message, and the headers travel as message attributes. SNS takes a message of up to 256 KiB. SNS is a publish target only: the service reads the queues subscribed to the topic. A queue joins a topic through subscribe_queue_to_topic, or through the operator's own provisioning. Either way, SNS delivers to the queue only when the queue's access policy lets the topic send to it, and subscribe_queue_to_topic adds that statement itself.

The dependency line: ruststream-sqs-sns = { version = "0.7", features = ["sns"] } The notification names its topic, so the handler answers with a bare reply clause. Macros Manual examples/sns_fanout.rs /// The notification the topic fans out. It names the topic, so the handler answers with a bare /// `reply` clause. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders-events")] struct OrderPlaced { id: u64, } #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("orders").create_if_missing(), reply)] async fn accept(order: &PlaceOrder) -> OrderPlaced { tracing::info!(order.id, "order accepted"); OrderPlaced { id: order.id } } examples/manual/sns_fanout.rs /// The notification the topic fans out. It names the topic, so the reply takes no destination /// at the mount site. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[outgoing(name = "orders-events")] struct OrderPlaced { id: u64, } struct Accept; impl Handle<PlaceOrder, OrderPlaced> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &PlaceOrder, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<OrderPlaced, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order accepted"); ready(Ok(OrderPlaced { id: order.id })) } } The mount site binds the reply position to SnsPublish, and billing and shipping each receive the order. fans_out_to names the queues an operator subscribed to a topic, so a test sees every queue the topic delivers to. A queue the service subscribes itself, through subscribe_queue_to_topic, is known to the broker. A queue an operator subscribed in AWS is known only to AWS. The step names those queues on the policy, and they apply to every topic the position publishes to. In process the account subscribes them to the topic before the publish, as the operator did. A live test waits for the subscription of each named queue to handle its copy. A queue SNS refuses, such as a FIFO queue on a standard topic, fails the publish. The step exists with the crate's testing feature, which a service enables in its [dev-dependencies]. The service builds the policy with the step under #[cfg(test)], which holds in the build of the tests beside its code. A production build neither has the step nor calls it. A test under tests/ builds the service without cfg(test). There the service gates the step on a feature of its own that enables ruststream-sqs-sns/testing, and the tests run with that feature.

The dependency line: [dev-dependencies] ruststream-sqs-sns = { version = "0.7", features = ["sns", "testing"] } The operator subscribed billing to orders-events, and the test build of the policy says so. The test build names the queue the operator subscribed. fn announcements() -> SnsPublish { let policy = SnsPublish::default(); #[cfg(test)] let policy = policy.fans_out_to(["billing"]); policy } fn service(broker: SqsBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(accept).out_reply(announcements()); b.include(bill); }) } examples/manual/sqs_sns_fans_out_to.rs /// The topic's policy. The test build names the queue the operator subscribed. fn announcements() -> SnsPublish { let policy = SnsPublish::default(); #[cfg(test)] let policy = policy.fans_out_to(["billing"]); policy } fn service(broker: SqsBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).reply().build()) .out_reply(announcements()); b.include(subscriber("billing", Bill).build()); }) }

subscribe_queue_to_topic subscribes a queue to a topic with raw message delivery, so payloads and headers arrive as plain SQS messages. The call takes a topic, by name or ARN, and a queue, by name or URL. A topic name resolves through CreateTopic, so a missing topic comes into being; the queue has to exist. With raw message delivery the notification's message is the queue message's body, and its attributes are the queue message's attributes. A handler on the queue therefore decodes the same payload and reads the same headers a publish to the queue would give it. SNS delivers to a queue only when the queue's access policy lets the topic send to it. Before it subscribes, the call adds that statement to the queue's policy: sqs:SendMessage for the SNS service, limited to this topic through aws:SourceArn. The statements already in the policy stay as they are. A policy that already grants the topic is not written again, so the call is safe on every start. SQS has no conditional write of a policy, so two services that grant different topics on one queue at the same moment can lose one of the grants. A policy that cannot be read or written fails the call with SqsError::QueuePolicy. The call needs sns:CreateTopic and sns:Subscribe on the topic, and sqs:GetQueueUrl, sqs:GetQueueAttributes and sqs:SetQueueAttributes on the queue (permissions). The method belongs to the connected broker, ConnectedSqsBroker. A service reaches it from an after_startup hook: it clones the app's broker before the app takes it, and the hook connects the clone. A clone connects through the connection the app's broker already holds, so in a test the call reaches the in-process account. By the time the hook runs, the subscriptions have opened their queues, create_if_missing ones included. SNS refuses a FIFO queue on a standard topic, and the call fails with SqsError::Admin. In production the topic and its subscriptions are often infrastructure that an operator provisions. A test of such a service names those queues on the policy with fans_out_to.

The hook subscribes both queues to the topic the reply fans out from. Macros Manual examples/sns_fanout.rs /// Subscribes both queues to the topic. The subscriptions have opened the queues by the time a /// startup hook runs. async fn wire_topology(broker: SqsBroker) -> io::Result<()> { let connected = broker.connect().await.map_err(io::Error::other)?; for queue in ["billing", "shipping"] { connected .subscribe_queue_to_topic("orders-events", queue) .await .map_err(io::Error::other)?; } Ok(()) } examples/manual/sns_fanout.rs /// Subscribes both queues to the topic. The subscriptions have opened the queues by the time a /// startup hook runs. async fn wire_topology(broker: SqsBroker) -> io::Result<()> { let connected = broker.connect().await.map_err(io::Error::other)?; for queue in ["billing", "shipping"] { connected .subscribe_queue_to_topic("orders-events", queue) .await .map_err(io::Error::other)?; } Ok(()) }

A queue name in #[subscriber] long-polls that queue; SqsQueue carries every other setting of the subscription. #[subscriber("orders")] reads the queue orders. The name resolves to the queue's URL through GetQueueUrl once, when the subscription opens. A bare name takes the descriptor's defaults: a 20 second long poll and the queue's own visibility timeout. #[subscriber(SqsQueue)] fixes the kind and leaves the queue to the mount site: b.include(audit.name("audit-eu")) reads audit-eu, so one definition serves several queues. SQS takes only [A-Za-z0-9_-] in a queue name, so every other character of the name becomes - on the way, and a .fifo suffix survives: order.events reads the queue order-events. Two subscriptions on one queue compete for its messages, and each message goes to one of them. A subscription receives at most one batch ahead of its handler. A queue that does not exist stops the service at startup, unless the subscription creates it. Once the service runs, a queue deleted under a subscription ends that subscription, and any other receive error is retried after one second. The manual form passes the name to subscriber(name, body), and Unnamed<SqsQueue> in place of the name leaves it to name at the mount site.

A slice handler gets one ReceiveMessage worth of messages; batch(n) becomes MaxNumberOfMessages, capped at ten. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. ReceiveMessage returns several messages per call, so the size becomes its MaxNumberOfMessages and one receive is one batch. Nothing buffers in the service. A batch holds what the queue had at that moment, so a quiet queue yields batches of one. A batch is never empty: a long poll that runs out hands the handler nothing. SQS returns at most ten messages per receive, so a larger size becomes ten, and the subscription logs that once. One outcome settles every message of the batch. A Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles message i with outcome i. A single-message handler also receives up to ten messages per call, because SQS bills per request, and gets them one at a time; workers(n) decides how many run at once. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>, where Ok(()) acknowledges the batch and Err(outcomes) settles each message.

create_if_missing() creates the queue at startup when it is missing; a .fifo name creates a FIFO queue, and a dead-letter queue is created too. The subscription calls CreateQueue when it opens and the account does not have the queue yet. Without the step, a missing queue stops the service at startup. A name that ends in .fifo creates a FIFO queue with content-based deduplication. A dead-letter queue the registration declares is created the same way. Every other attribute of a new queue keeps the SQS default, a 30 second visibility timeout among them. The step needs the sqs:CreateQueue permission. It suits a local stack and a test; production queues are usually managed as infrastructure. In process every queue a service names exists already, so the step shows its effect in a live test. The step is on SqsQueue, and on the mount chain through SqsSubscription::create_if_missing, as in the example.

A drafts queue the service opens itself on a fresh stack. A .fifo queue hands out each message group in order and holds a group back while one of its messages is in flight. A queue whose name ends in .fifo is a FIFO queue, and a subscription reads it like any other queue. Every message on it belongs to a message group, which the producer names: the group_id step, the partition key header, or default when it names neither. The queue hands out the messages of a group in the order they were sent. While a message of a group is in flight, the queue holds the rest of that group back until the message is deleted or its visibility lapses. Other groups go on meanwhile. So a retry brings the same message back before the next one of its group. The delivery carries its group in PARTITION_KEY_HEADER. A FIFO queue drops a message whose deduplication id it has seen in the last five minutes. A FIFO queue takes a FIFO dead-letter queue, and create_if_missing on a .fifo name creates a FIFO queue. In process the account keeps the same order and holds a group back the same way.

SqsQueue describes one subscription by queue name or URL, with its long poll, visibility timeout and queue creation. SqsQueue::new takes a queue name or a queue URL (https://sqs...). A name resolves through GetQueueUrl once, when the subscription opens; a URL is used as it is. Three steps set the rest, and each has a default: wait (20 seconds), visibility (the queue's own timeout) and create_if_missing (off). The descriptor goes where the name goes, as the first argument of #[subscriber(..)]. The subscription's name is what the descriptor names: a test reads its deliveries under that name. A descriptor that cannot form a subscription stops the service at startup with SqsError::InvalidQueue, before any call to AWS: an empty name, a wait over 20 seconds, or a visibility outside one second to twelve hours. The same three steps are on the mount chain through SqsSubscription. The manual form builds the descriptor and hands it to the chain with map_source.

SqsSubscription puts the queue steps on the mount chain, after the framework's own steps such as batch(n) and name. The steps are those of SqsQueue: wait, visibility and create_if_missing. They chain after a framework step: a batch size, a name for a definition that fixed only the kind, or workers(n). A step at the mount site changes the descriptor the attribute built, so it wins over the attribute's value. The steps exist only on the chain of a subscription whose source is an SqsQueue, so they never reach another broker's subscription. The trait comes with the crate's prelude. In the manual form the steps follow map_source or name.

visibility(duration) sets how long a received message stays hidden; the crate re-arms it halfway through each timeout while the handler runs. The visibility timeout is what each receive asks for: how long a received message stays hidden from every other receive. SQS counts the timeout in whole seconds, from one second to twelve hours. A value outside that range stops the service at startup with SqsError::InvalidQueue. A fraction above one second rounds up to the next whole second, so a message never comes back sooner than the timeout asked for. A subscription that names none takes the queue's own timeout, which it reads once with GetQueueAttributes when it opens, so it needs the sqs:GetQueueAttributes permission. A handler may take longer than the timeout. While a handler holds a delivery, the crate re-arms the timeout halfway through each period with ChangeMessageVisibility, so no other consumer receives the message in the meantime. The other half of the period is left for the call to reach the queue, so a one-second timeout is re-armed every half second. SQS keeps a message hidden for at most twelve hours from its receive, and an extension does not restart them. A handler that holds a delivery that long gets one last extension to the end of the twelve hours and a warning in the log; after that the queue hands the message to another consumer. The timeout also decides how soon an abandoned delivery comes back: a message dropped unsettled, or one a stopped process held, is received again once the timeout lapses. In process, a subscription that names no timeout gets the 30 seconds of a new queue; the timeout an operator set on a queue shows only in a live test. The step is on SqsQueue, and on the mount chain through SqsSubscription::visibility, as in the example.

A report takes five seconds to render, and a receive hides it for two; the report is still handled once. Macros Manual examples/sqs_subscriptions_visibility.rs /// Rendering a report takes longer than the two seconds a receive hides it for. The crate /// re-arms the visibility every second while the handler runs, so no other consumer gets the /// report in the meantime. #[subscriber(SqsQueue)] async fn publish_report(report: &Report) -> HandlerOutcome { render(report).await; tracing::info!(report.id, "report published"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: SqsBroker, queue: String) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reports", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( publish_report .name(queue) .visibility(Duration::from_secs(2)), ); }) } examples/manual/sqs_subscriptions_visibility.rs /// Rendering a report takes longer than the two seconds a receive hides it for. The crate /// re-arms the visibility every second while the handler runs, so no other consumer gets the /// report in the meantime. struct PublishReport; impl Handle<Report> for PublishReport { async fn handle( &self, report: &Report, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { render(report).await; tracing::info!(report.id, "report published"); Ok(()) } } fn service(broker: SqsBroker, queue: String) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reports", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber(Unnamed::<SqsQueue>::new(), PublishReport) .build() .name(queue) .visibility(Duration::from_secs(2)), ); }) }

wait(duration) sets how long one receive waits for a message, 20 seconds by default and at most; a longer wait stops the service at startup. The wait is the WaitTimeSeconds of each ReceiveMessage: the long poll. A receive returns as soon as a message arrives, and returns empty when the wait runs out. An empty receive hands the handler nothing. A longer wait means fewer empty receives, and SQS bills per request. The default is the SQS maximum of 20 seconds, so a subscription that names no wait already polls as long as SQS allows. A wait over 20 seconds stops the service at startup with SqsError::InvalidQueue. A zero wait is short polling: each receive returns at once, with what a sample of the queue's servers holds. The step is on SqsQueue, and on the mount chain through SqsSubscription::wait.

Each receive on alerts waits up to five seconds. Macros Manual examples/sqs_subscriptions_wait.rs /// Each receive on `alerts` waits up to five seconds and returns as soon as an alert arrives. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("alerts").wait(Duration::from_secs(5)))] async fn page(alert: &Alert) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(alert.id, "on-call paged"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_subscriptions_wait.rs /// Each receive on `alerts` waits up to five seconds and returns as soon as an alert arrives. fn alerts() -> SqsQueue { SqsQueue::new("alerts").wait(Duration::from_secs(5)) } fn service(broker: SqsBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("alerts", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber("alerts", Page).build().map_source(|_| alerts())); }) }

TestApp::start connects SqsBroker to an in-process account with queues, visibility, receive counts, redrive, FIFO groups and topics. A test hands the harness the app main runs, unchanged, and addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<SqsBroker>(). The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode, and turns on the core's harness with it. The account has no settings of its own. Its queue URLs are built on the broker's endpoint and region, and every setting a queue has comes from the service's descriptors. Every queue and topic the service names exists in it. The account keeps SQS's semantics. A queue hands each message to one of its subscriptions, and one receive returns at most ten messages. A received message stays invisible until it is deleted or its visibility timeout lapses; a descriptor that names no visibility gets the 30 seconds of a new queue. The receive count rises with every receive, and a redrive policy moves a message whose receives ran out to the dead-letter queue. A FIFO group waits while one of its messages is in flight, and a deduplication id is remembered for five minutes. With sns, a topic delivers a copy to every queue subscribed to it. The account refuses what SQS and SNS refuse: more than ten headers, a header name the service does not take, an empty body or header value, a message over the size limit, a queue name over 80 characters, a dead-letter queue of the other kind, a maxReceiveCount over 1000, a visibility that would end more than twelve hours after the receive, and a FIFO queue on a standard topic. A publish through the harness that SQS would refuse fails the test. A standard queue keeps the order of its messages here, which SQS does not promise. A message sent to a queue no subscription reads is dropped. A publish through the harness returns once every handler it woke has settled. tb.advance(..), on a clock paused with #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)], moves past a visibility timeout or a deferred retry. What belongs to a running service, such as a queue an operator configured, is for a live test.

The dependency line: [dev-dependencies] ruststream-sqs-sns = { version = "0.7", features = ["testing"] } The first test publishes a payment and reads how the handler settled it. TestApp::start_live runs the same test body against LocalStack or AWS, for what belongs to the service: queues, timeouts, credentials. It connects the broker through its ordinary connect, so every subscription resolves its queue on the stack and every request is signed. The body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what was published to it. The wait lasts ten seconds at most, and start_live_within sets another bound. The live mode is for what the in-process account leaves to the service: a message kept on a queue no subscription reads, the visibility timeout an operator set on a queue, the queues and topics the service expects to find without creating them, and credentials. A stack keeps what earlier runs left in it, so each run names its queues uniquely, and creates them with create_if_missing or before the app starts. In the example, live::endpoint returns the stack's address from SQS_TEST_ENDPOINT, and the test returns early without one, so cargo test passes on a machine with no stack. A job that stood a stack up sets RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE=1, and a missing address then fails the test instead of skipping it. The repository's stand is LocalStack in docker-compose.test.yml, which just brokers-up starts.

The two tests share one body: one in process, one against the stack at SQS_TEST_ENDPOINT. Это руководство показывает, что каждый исход обработчика делает с сообщением SQS, как обработчик остаётся корректным, когда сообщение приходит дважды, и как завершается пакет. SQS доставляет хотя бы один раз. Полученное сообщение остаётся в очереди, невидимое, пока потребитель его не удалит. Стандартная очередь может также доставить сообщение дважды и не в том порядке, в каком его отправили (AWS: доставка at-least-once). Пример - платёжный сервис, который проводит платежи по книге учёта и выплачивает возвраты.

Каждый исход - один вызов SQS для сообщения, которое получил обработчик: Исход Вызов SQS Что происходит с сообщением ack DeleteMessage оно покидает очередь drop DeleteMessage оно покидает очередь: в SQS нет вызова, который отвергает сообщение и сохраняет его retry ChangeMessageVisibility в ноль оно сразу выдаётся повторно retry_after ChangeMessageVisibility на задержку оно выдаётся повторно, когда задержка заканчивается Сообщение, которое обработчик так и не завершил, потому что процесс остановился посреди работы, вызова не получает. Оно возвращается, когда истекает его тайм-аут видимости. Поэтому обработчик выполняет работу до исхода, а сообщение удаляется только после того, как работа сделана.

Макросы Вручную src/main.rs /// How long a payment on an account under review waits before the next try. const REVIEW: Duration = Duration::from_secs(60); /// The receive after which a payment under review is given up. const LAST_RECEIVE: u32 = 3; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "payments")] struct Payment { id: u64, account: String, amount_cents: u64, under_review: bool, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "ledger-entries")] struct Entry { payment: u64, account: String, amount_cents: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Entry)] struct Entries; /// The ids of the payments already booked. #[derive(Debug, Default, Clone)] struct Ledger { booked: Arc<Mutex<HashSet<u64>>>, } #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("payments"))] async fn book( payment: &Payment, ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Ledger>, Out(entries): Out<impl Publisher, Entries>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { // SQS counts the receives of a message, this one included. let receives: u32 = ctx .headers() .get_str(RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER) .and_then(|count| count.parse().ok()) .unwrap_or(1); if payment.under_review { if receives >= LAST_RECEIVE { tracing::error!(payment.id, receives, "payment dropped, still under review"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(REVIEW); } let booked = Arc::clone(&ctx.state().booked); if booked .lock() .unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner) .contains(&payment.id) { tracing::info!(payment.id, receives, "payment already booked"); return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } let entry = Entry { payment: payment.id, account: payment.account.clone(), amount_cents: payment.amount_cents, }; if entries.message(&entry).publish().await.is_err() { // Nothing is booked yet: the payment comes back and the work runs again. return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } booked .lock() .unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner) .insert(payment.id); tracing::info!(payment.id, "payment booked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// How long a payment on an account under review waits before the next try. const REVIEW: Duration = Duration::from_secs(60); /// The receive after which a payment under review is given up. const LAST_RECEIVE: u32 = 3; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Payment { id: u64, account: String, amount_cents: u64, under_review: bool, } impl OutgoingDestination for Payment { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "payments"; } impl MessageHeaders for Payment { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Payment { const NAME: &'static str = "Payment"; } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Entry { payment: u64, account: String, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Entry { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "ledger-entries"; } impl MessageHeaders for Entry { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Entry { const NAME: &'static str = "Entry"; } struct Entries; impl OutSlot for Entries { const NAME: &'static str = "Entries"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Entries> for Entry {} /// The ids of the payments already booked. #[derive(Debug, Default, Clone)] struct Ledger { booked: Arc<Mutex<HashSet<u64>>>, } struct Book; impl<Wire> Handle<Payment, (), Outs<(Wire,)>, (), Ledger> for Book where Wire: OutEntry<Entries, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, outs: &Outs<(Wire,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Ledger>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { // SQS counts the receives of a message, this one included. let receives: u32 = ctx .headers() .get_str(RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER) .and_then(|count| count.parse().ok()) .unwrap_or(1); if payment.under_review { if receives >= LAST_RECEIVE { tracing::error!(payment.id, receives, "payment dropped, still under review"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(REVIEW)); } let booked = Arc::clone(&ctx.state().booked); if booked .lock() .unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner) .contains(&payment.id) { tracing::info!(payment.id, receives, "payment already booked"); return Ok(()); } let entry = Entry { payment: payment.id, account: payment.account.clone(), amount_cents: payment.amount_cents, }; if outs.get(Entries).message(&entry).publish().await.is_err() { // Nothing is booked yet: the payment comes back and the work runs again. return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } booked .lock() .unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner) .insert(payment.id); tracing::info!(payment.id, "payment booked"); Ok(()) } } book записывает в книгу учёта проводку платежа и затем подтверждает его. Платёж, который SQS доставил второй раз, находится среди проведённых идентификаторов и подтверждается без второй проводки. Множество в состоянии приложения заменяет хранилище, в котором сервис держит проведённые идентификаторы; идентификатор - собственный идентификатор платежа, а не идентификатор сообщения SQS, потому что отправитель, который отправил дважды, отправил два сообщения. Когда проводку не удаётся опубликовать, ничего не проводится, и retry возвращает платёж для новой попытки. Обработчик читает RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER - собственный ApproximateReceiveCount очереди. Он учитывает и текущее получение, поэтому у первой доставки там 1. Платёж по счёту на проверке ждёт минуту через retry_after, а на третьем получении обработчик сдаётся и отбрасывает его. Как сама очередь ограничивает число получений и сохраняет то, что не удалось обработать, показывает руководство Переобработка и DLQ.

/// How long a refund waits for approval before it is looked at again. const APPROVAL: Duration = Duration::from_secs(300); /// Settles each refund of a batch on its own: a small refund is paid and deleted, a large one /// waits on the queue for its approval. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("refunds"))] async fn settle_refunds(refunds: &[Refund]) -> Vec<HandlerOutcome> { refunds .iter() .map(|refund| { if refund.amount_cents > APPROVAL_LIMIT_CENTS { tracing::info!(refund.payment, "refund waits for approval"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(APPROVAL) } else { tracing::info!(refund.payment, refund.amount_cents, "refund paid"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } }) .collect() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Refund { payment: u64, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Refund { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "refunds"; } impl MessageHeaders for Refund { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Refund { const NAME: &'static str = "Refund"; } /// The largest refund paid without a person's approval. const APPROVAL_LIMIT_CENTS: u64 = 50_000; /// How long a refund waits for approval before it is looked at again. const APPROVAL: Duration = Duration::from_secs(300); /// Settles each refund of a batch on its own: a small refund is paid and deleted, a large one /// waits on the queue for its approval. struct SettleRefunds; impl Handle<[Refund], (), (), (), Ledger> for SettleRefunds { fn handle( &self, refunds: &[Refund], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Ledger>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { let outcomes: Vec<HandlerOutcome> = refunds .iter() .map(|refund| { if refund.amount_cents > APPROVAL_LIMIT_CENTS { tracing::info!(refund.payment, "refund waits for approval"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(APPROVAL) } else { tracing::info!(refund.payment, refund.amount_cents, "refund paid"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } }) .collect(); ready(Err(outcomes)) } } Обработчик пакетов возвращает по одному исходу на сообщение, в порядке среза. Каждый исход - отдельный вызов для своего сообщения. Здесь мелкие возвраты удаляются, а крупный остаётся в очереди и через пять минут возвращается один. Обработчик пакетов, который возвращает один исход, завершает им каждое сообщение пакета.

Макросы Вручную src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = Ledger> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Ledger::default())) .with_broker( SqsBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), |b| { b.include(book).out(Entries, Publish::default()).build(); b.include(settle_refunds.batch(nonzero!(10))); }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = Ledger> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Ledger::default())) .with_broker( SqsBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), |b| { b.include( subscriber("payments", Book) .map_source(|_| SqsQueue::new("payments")) .build(), ) .out(Entries, Publish::default()) .build(); b.include( subscriber("refunds", SettleRefunds) .batch(nonzero!(10)) .map_source(|_| SqsQueue::new("refunds")) .build(), ); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } book публикует проводки через слот Entries, привязанный к издателю очереди в точке монтирования. Очередь FIFO в течение пяти минут отбрасывает повторную отправку с тем же идентификатором дедупликации, и это не даёт отправителю отправить одно сообщение дважды; это показывает руководство Очереди FIFO. Обработчик на стандартной очереди всё равно ведёт собственный учёт того, что уже сделал. Тесты в файле примера доставляют платёж дважды, на остановленных часах дают платежу на проверке исчерпать получения и отправляют три возврата одним пакетом. Обвязку разбирает руководство Тестирование сервиса на SQS.

Это руководство читает очереди SQS: длинный опрос, тайм-аут видимости медленного обработчика, параллельные обработчики, пакеты и один обработчик на нескольких очередях. Пример - сервис склада. Он упаковывает заказы, проводит платежи и записывает изменения заказов.

Макросы Вручную src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders")] struct Order { id: u64, items: u32, } /// Packs an order. Packing takes up to a minute, so each receive asks for a minute of /// visibility, and four orders are packed at once. #[subscriber( SqsQueue::new("orders") .visibility(Duration::from_secs(60)) .create_if_missing(), workers(4) )] async fn pack(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, order.items, "order packed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, items: u32, } impl OutgoingDestination for Order { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "orders"; } impl MessageHeaders for Order { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Order { const NAME: &'static str = "Order"; } /// Packs an order. struct Pack; impl Handle<Order> for Pack { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, order.items, "order packed"); ready(Ok(())) } } Подписка опрашивает свою очередь длинным опросом через ReceiveMessage. Каждый вызов ждёт сообщения до 20 секунд - дольше SQS не позволяет. wait задаёт более короткое ожидание. Очередь называют по имени или по URL, а имя разрешается через GetQueueUrl один раз, при старте. Подписка, которая обрабатывает сообщения по одному, всё равно запрашивает до десяти сообщений за вызов, потому что SQS берёт плату за запросы. Обработчику она отдаёт их по одному. Пока обработчик работает, фоновая задача получает следующий пакет и никогда не опережает его больше чем на один пакет.

Полученное сообщение остаётся невидимым для других потребителей на время тайм-аута видимости очереди. Если к этому времени его не удалили, SQS выдаёт его повторно. visibility запрашивает при каждом получении собственный тайм-аут, от одной секунды до двенадцати часов. SQS считает его в целых секундах, поэтому доля секунды округляется вверх. pack запрашивает минуту. Без этого шага подписка один раз, при открытии, читает собственный тайм-аут очереди. Обработчик может работать дольше тайм-аута. Пока доставка не завершена, крейт продлевает её видимость в середине каждого тайм-аута, поэтому сообщение медленного обработчика не достаётся другому потребителю. SQS скрывает сообщение не дольше двенадцати часов с момента получения. Если обработчик работает так долго, крейт продлевает видимость последний раз до конца этих двенадцати часов и пишет предупреждение в журнал, а затем сообщение получает другой потребитель.

workers(4) выполняет до четырёх доставок из orders одновременно. Четыре обработчика делят сообщения, которые возвращает каждое получение. У стандартной очереди нет порядка, который нужно сохранять, поэтому больше ничего не требуется. Очереди FIFO сохраняют порядок группы сообщений с помощью workers(n, by_key).

Макросы Вручную src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "payments")] struct Payment { order: u64, amount_cents: u64, } /// Books the payments one receive returned, in one write to the ledger. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("payments"))] async fn reconcile(payments: &[Payment]) -> HandlerOutcome { let total: u64 = payments.iter().map(|payment| payment.amount_cents).sum(); tracing::info!(count = payments.len(), total, "payments booked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Payment { order: u64, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Payment { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "payments"; } impl MessageHeaders for Payment { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Payment { const NAME: &'static str = "Payment"; } /// Books the payments one receive returned, in one write to the ledger. struct Reconcile; impl Handle<[Payment]> for Reconcile { fn handle( &self, payments: &[Payment], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { let total: u64 = payments.iter().map(|payment| payment.amount_cents).sum(); tracing::info!(count = payments.len(), total, "payments booked"); ready(Ok(())) } } Обработчик, который принимает срез, - обработчик пакетов. Размер, заданный в его точке монтирования, становится MaxNumberOfMessages, поэтому одно получение - это один пакет. Пакет содержит то, что было в очереди в этот момент, а длинный опрос, который ничего не вернул, пакета не даёт. ReceiveMessage возвращает не больше десяти сообщений, поэтому больший размер снижается до десяти, и сервис один раз пишет об этом в журнал. Каждое сообщение пакета завершается отдельно; исходы показывает руководство Подтверждение.

Макросы Вручную src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] struct Change { order: u64, by: String, } /// Records a change to an order. The definition fixes the kind of queue and leaves its name /// to the mount site. #[subscriber(SqsQueue)] async fn audit(change: &Change) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(change.order, change.by, "change recorded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Change { order: u64, by: String, } impl OutgoingDestination for Change { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Change { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Change { const NAME: &'static str = "Change"; } /// Records a change to an order, on whichever queue it is mounted. struct Audit; impl Handle<Change> for Audit { fn handle( &self, change: &Change, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(change.order, change.by, "change recorded"); ready(Ok(())) } } #[subscriber(SqsQueue)] фиксирует вид источника и оставляет имя очереди открытым. Точка монтирования называет его через .name(..), по разу на каждую очередь.

Макросы Вручную src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("warehouse", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqsBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), |b| { b.include(pack); // Up to ten payments per call: one receive is one batch. b.include( reconcile .batch(nonzero!(10)) .wait(Duration::from_secs(20)) .create_if_missing(), ); // One definition, two queues. b.include(audit.name("audit-eu").create_if_missing()); b.include(audit.name("audit-us").create_if_missing()); }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("warehouse", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqsBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), |b| { // A minute of visibility per receive, four orders packed at once. b.include( subscriber("orders", Pack) .map_source(|_| { SqsQueue::new("orders") .visibility(Duration::from_secs(60)) .create_if_missing() }) .workers(nonzero!(4)) .build(), ); // Up to ten payments per call: one receive is one batch. b.include( subscriber("payments", Reconcile) .batch(nonzero!(10)) .map_source(|_| { SqsQueue::new("payments") .wait(Duration::from_secs(20)) .create_if_missing() }) .build(), ); // One handler, two queues. for queue in ["audit-eu", "audit-us"] { b.include( subscriber(queue, Audit) .map_source(|_| SqsQueue::new(queue).create_if_missing()) .build(), ); } }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } Шаги очереди тоже задаются в точке монтирования, после шагов самого фреймворка, через SqsSubscription. Пустое имя очереди, ожидание дольше 20 секунд или видимость вне допустимого диапазона останавливают сервис при старте с ошибкой SqsError::InvalidQueue ещё до обращения к AWS. Имя может содержать символы, которых SQS не принимает: каждый символ вне A-Z, a-z, 0-9, _ и - заменяется на -, а суффикс .fifo сохраняется. create_if_missing создаёт очередь, которой нет. Сервис в промышленной эксплуатации обычно получает очереди от своей инфраструктуры и опускает этот шаг; тогда отсутствующая очередь останавливает его при старте.

Каждый атрибут сообщения приходит в доставке заголовком, а каждый заголовок публикации уходит атрибутом. Два заголовка принадлежат самому крейту. RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER хранит счётчик получений сообщения в очереди. PARTITION_KEY_HEADER хранит группу сообщений очереди FIFO. Тело SQS - это текст, поэтому двоичная полезная нагрузка передаётся в кодировке base64 с атрибутом-меткой и приходит уже декодированной. Base64 увеличивает такую нагрузку на треть, а сообщение больше предельного размера SQS отвергает. Тесты в файле примера публикуют в приложение внутри процесса заказы, платежи и изменения. Обвязку разбирает руководство Тестирование сервиса на SQS.

Это руководство публикует сообщение в тему SNS один раз, а SNS доставляет копию в каждую очередь SQS, подписанную на эту тему. Связка SNS и SQS - это способ, которым сервисы AWS доставляют сообщения всем подписчикам разом: одна тема и по очереди на каждого потребителя. Крейт публикует в темы, а каждую очередь за темой сервис читает обычным образом. Для публикации в SNS нужна фича sns: Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream-sqs-sns = { version = "0.7", features = ["sns"] } Пример - магазин. Он принимает заказ и объявляет о нём в теме, а оплата и доставка читают это объявление каждая из своей очереди.
